Tad DeHaven 11 月 12 日，特朗普总统表示，英伟达“只有一个人”取代黄仁勋。他指的是苹果前首席执行官蒂姆·库克。 11 天后，英伟达宣布黄仁勋复职，特朗普对 CNBC 表示，“我做了这笔交易。”  为什么总统要达成这样的协议？黄在承认与一名涉嫌与中国情报部门有联系的女性有染后辞职。两位英伟达股东敦促董事会对让他回归持开放态度。一名英伟达员工建立了一个网站，人们可以在上面签署一封呼吁他回归的信。股东和员工完全有权向董事们提出自己的理由，而董事们在 11 月 17 日告诉投资者，他们无意恢复黄的职位。英伟达董事会也有充分的理由询问联邦官员对可疑情报行动的了解。根据董事会的声明，政府的回答缓解了他们对国家安全的担忧。他们还会见了黄，并表示他们对他能够领导公司感到满意，尽管他们自己的调查仍在进行中。但特朗普向他们施压，要求他们恢复黄的职位，从而越界了。任何仍然认为让黄回来是一个错误的董事都被迫权衡英伟达违抗总统可能付出的代价。这让人有理由怀疑英伟达董事会恢复黄仁勋的决定是否真的正确。如果董事会的内部调查发现更多涉及黄的令人不安的信息，会发生什么？
特朗普宣称其复职对美国繁荣至关重要，它会不愿意对这位首席执行官采取行动吗？当 CNBC 的萨拉·艾森问特朗普他的底线在哪里时，他回答说：“我是为了国家而这样做。”用特朗普的话说，美国的繁荣取决于黄仁勋掌管英伟达。难怪吉姆·克莱默在同一次电话会议上询问，如果该公司陷入财务困境，华盛顿是否会提供援助。特朗普表示，他认为事情不会发展到这个地步，但他正在回答有关一家上季度盈利 653 亿美元的公司的救助问题。我们已经看到，当华盛顿认定一家公司太重要而不能倒闭时，董事会会发生什么。 2009年，通用汽车依靠联邦救助维持生存，奥巴马政府罢免了首席执行官里克·瓦格纳，并任命了他的继任者弗里茨·亨德森。亨德森后来告诉调查人员，通用汽车的董事认为财政部篡夺了他们选择首席执行官的权力。美国政府已经对英伟达的业务拥有足够的发言权，可以要求削减对中国的某些芯片销售。下次特朗普向黄求助时，他可以提醒黄是谁帮助他重新获得了工作。正如我的同事斯科特·林西科姆 (Scott Lincicome) 今天指出的那样，这种干预的经济成本比周一英伟达股价的上涨更难以看出。以英特尔为例。 2025 年 8 月，特朗普因首席执行官陈立武 (Lip-Bu Tan) 与中国的关系而要求他辞职。
谭匆匆赶到白宫，特朗普说他在那里告诉他，“如果你聪明的话，就把你公司 10% 的股份交给美国。”谭保住了他的工作，联邦政府成为英特尔股东。同月，蒂姆·库克前往白宫寻求苹果的关税豁免。正如斯科特所记录的那样，据报道，特朗普和商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克向库克施压，要求英特尔生产一些苹果芯片。苹果获得了豁免。十个月后，特朗普将他所说的苹果和英特尔之间的交易归功于自己。 “我们是

【原文 English Original】
Tad DeHaven On November 12, President Trump said there was “only one man” to replace Jensen Huang at Nvidia. He meant former Apple CEO Tim Cook. Eleven days later, Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement, and Trump told CNBC , “I made the deal.”  Why was that the president’s deal to make? Huang resigned after acknowledging an affair with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Two Nvidia shareholders urged the board to keep an open mind about bringing him back. An Nvidia employee set up a website where people could sign a letter calling for his return. Shareholders and employees had every right to make their case to the directors, who had told investors on November 17 that they had no intention of reinstating Huang. Nvidia’s board also had good reason to ask federal officials what they knew about the suspected intelligence operation. The government’s answer eased their national security concerns, according to the board’s statement . They also met with Huang and said they were satisfied that he could lead the company, though their own investigation remains open.  But Trump crossed the line by pressuring them to reinstate Huang. Any director who still thought it was a mistake to bring back Huang was forced to weigh what it might cost Nvidia to defy the president. That makes it fair to wonder whether Nvidia’s board was truly kosher with reinstating Huang. What happens if the board’s internal investigation turns up more troubling information involving Huang? Will it be reluctant to act against a CEO whose reinstatement Trump declared essential to American prosperity?  When CNBC’s Sara Eisen asked Trump where he drew the line, he replied, “I’m doing it for the country.” In Trump’s telling , American prosperity depends on having Huang at the helm of Nvidia. Little wonder that Jim Cramer asked on the same call whether Washington would come to the company’s aid if it got into financial trouble. Trump said he didn’t think it would come to that, but here he was fielding a bailout question about a company that earned $65.3 billion last quarter. We’ve seen what happens to a board when Washington decides a company is too important to fail. In 2009, while General Motors depended on a federal bailout to stay afloat, the Obama administration ousted CEO Rick Wagoner and appointed his successor, Fritz Henderson. Henderson later told investigators that GM’s directors felt Treasury had usurped their authority to choose the CEO. The administration already has enough say over Nvidia’s business to claim a cut of certain chip sales to China. And the next time Trump asks Huang for a favor, he can remind him who helped get him his job back. As my colleague Scott Lincicome pointed out today , the economic costs of this kind of interference are harder to see than Monday’s jump in Nvidia’s share price.  Take Intel . In August 2025, Trump called on CEO Lip-Bu Tan to resign over Tan’s ties to China. Tan scurried to the White House, where Trump says he told him , “If you’re smart, give the United States of America 10 percent of your company.” Tan kept his job, and the federal government became an Intel shareholder.  That same month, Tim Cook went to the White House seeking a tariff exemption for Apple. As Scott has documented , Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly pressed Cook to have Intel make some of Apple’s chips. Apple got its exemption. Ten months later, Trump took credit for what he described as a deal between Apple and Intel. “We want capital flowing to companies for commercial reasons,” Scott told the New York Times . Good luck with that when the president is out recruiting customers for a company in the federal portfolio . “Investors have grown accustomed to President Trump influencing the prospects of different companies, whether it’s rare earth metals, energy, and chips,” JoAnne Feeney, a portfolio manager at Advisors Capital Management, told Bloomberg . “It certainly has made investing more complicated because it has to be factored into which stocks you choose to hold. It’s not the way the US capitalistic system is designed.” No, it’s not .  Huang is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3 about chip exports. Congress is already asking the administration which officials weighed in with Nvidia’s board and what they said to get Huang reinstated.  But Congress ought to keep Nvidia in mind as it considers the Senate’s defense authorization bill . Section 1051 would let the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital buy stakes in suppliers of critical minerals and other materials while barring its director from taking a board seat or obtaining other voting representation. Trump didn’t need a seat on Nvidia’s board to get its directors on the phone. Now imagine taking that call when the federal government is also one of your largest shareholders.

问答：什么是“公正过渡”的贝伦-安塔利亚机制？ 互动：追踪 COP31 气候峰会上的谈判文本 互动：谁在 COP31 气候变化峰会上想要什么 由于严重分歧阻碍了主席主导的协议达成一致，联合国气候变化框架公约主席西蒙·斯蒂尔表示“深感失望”，谈到了联合国气候进程的“改进、现代化和改革的范围”。尽管最后一场混乱的缔约方会议成为历史上最长的一次会议，但它并没有以完全失败告终，许多项目在闭幕全体会议上获得通过。其中包括为全球“公正转型”建立新“机制”的相当有限的或程序性的成果，以及对遭受气候灾难的国家的支持。不过，谈判之外还取得了一些进展，越来越多的国家联盟倡导“摆脱”化石燃料的“路线图”。随着主席国推动“电气化”成为关键主题，约 80 个国家还签署了到 2035 年确保 35% 的最终能源消耗来自电力的全球目标。在此，Carbon Brief 深入分析了安塔利亚会议在 COP31 谈判内外的所有关键成果。

Print article Share Article Contents Expand menu Close Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance . The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations. Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation. COP31 coverage Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31 Analysis: Which countries have sent the most delegates to COP31? Q&A: What is the Belém-Antalya mechanism for a ‘just transition’? Interactive: Tracking negotiating texts at the COP31 climate summit Interactive: Who wants what at the COP31 climate change summit With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process. Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary. These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “ mechanism ” for global “ just transitions ”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters. There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “ roadmaps ” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. With the presidency promoting “ electrification ” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations. (See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30 , COP29 , COP28 , COP27 , COP26 , COP25 , COP24 , COP23 , COP22 , COP21 and COP20 .) Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Cover decision COP reform Adaptation Finance Just transition work programme Loss and damage Gender Article 6 Agriculture and food security Mitigation work programme Response measures Action for climate empowerment Trade Second global stocktake Long-term goal review Guidance on NDCs Rio synergies Around the COP Fossil fuels Action agenda Global leaders Electrification China at COP31 Ocean Deforestation Methane New climate science Food and water NDCs Protests and access Road to COP32 and beyond Formal negotiations Turkish and Australian leadership Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges. Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted. Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer. Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years . In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”. COP31 president and Turkish minister Murat Kurum and COP31 “president of negotiations” and Australian minister Chris Bowen. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion. Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production. Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31. The first letter , written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October. The second letter , authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”. The third letter , published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “ action agenda ” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further. This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification .) The final letter , published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”. It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding: “At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.” The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . A crowded roadbridge near the COP31 entrance in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”. He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues. On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision .) At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down. On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations. Countries take part in a “divan” at COP31. Credit: UNFCCC / Flickr Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening. In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday. Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”. However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision .) On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge. Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.  In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.  They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.  An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”. As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. width: 64px; align-self: start; } } Membership Connect with our community Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.  Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious –  closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .)  While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised… Read more on CB Connect → This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations. The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target , as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels .) A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs. This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation .) It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”. Paragraph 36 of the second draft cover text. Source: UNFCCC . Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “ quid pro quo ” for the quantified electrification target. The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”. Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro. A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit. This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”. Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups. They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.) The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted. However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports. On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.” But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful. The UK told the closing plenary: “What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.” Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures.
