As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update on the state of the text failed to materialise.  Tuvalu’s Talia told a cramped press huddle that Pacific island nations had been waiting for the text since last night and were still willing to fight to get transitioning away from fossil fuels back in. Maina Vakafua Talia, Tuvalu’s climate minister, speaks to journalists. Credit: Sandro Basili / Alamy Stock Photo On Saturday evening, the fallout over fossil fuels intensified.  Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UG, AOSIS, AILAC and LDCs – approached the presidency as a united front to demand that transitioning away from fossil fuels featured in the final cover decision. One observer told Carbon Brief that such close cooperation between the EU and AOSIS is “unprecedented” at COP. They added that it might reflect the fact that Ireland, which currently holds the EU presidency, is working closely with Tuvalu on holding the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference next year. A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  This one also did not directly mention fossil fuels. However, it did “recall” the COP28 UAE consensus “in its entirety”, which itself includes a reference to a “just, orderly and equitable” transition away from fossil fuels. Carbon Brief contributing editor Dr Joanna Depledge wrote on LinkedIn that this oblique reference was “near meaningless”. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, many countries rejected the text – citing its failure to clearly reference transitioning away from fossil fuels as one of the key reasons. (See: Cover decision .) Action agenda Many issues that were intensely negotiated at COP31 – including the electrification goal and fossil-fuel phaseout – also featured in the “ action agenda ”. This is the part of the UN climate process that involves mobilising real-world climate action from non-state actors, including businesses, investors and civil-society groups.  It also covers voluntary actions taken by groups of countries beyond the COP negotiations. When the “Antalya pact” failed to materialise, the presidency’s action agenda package was one of its more substantial outputs.  In this closing remarks at COP31, after the headline negotiated outcome had collapsed, UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell reminded delegates: “This COP process has two tracks. And across the action agenda, COP31 has delivered real progress and concrete results.” With Australia overseeing negotiations, the action agenda was instead a priority for the Turkish presidency, which used COP31 to launch a variety of new projects and “ compacts ”. In a phrase familiar to attendees of previous COPs , Turkish COP31 president Murat Kurum said he wanted an “implementation COP” that would leave people saying: “Something changed in Antalya.” Delegates resting by a wall with the COP31 slogan “dialogue, consensus, action”. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Amid global conflict, struggling multilateralism and the imminent breaching of the 1.5C Paris Agreement goal, UN climate talks have repeatedly failed to reach consensus on vital issues. Some have, therefore , welcomed what the Brazilian COP30 presidency called “two-tier multilateralism”, in which parties try to find consensus where they can and, where they cannot, coalitions of willing nations and groups push more ambitious action forward. Kaveh Guilanpour , vice president for international strategies at the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions (C2ES), told Carbon Brief: “There’s a lot of inertia in the formal way of negotiating and we’re trying to find our way to whatever that new thing is, given the foundational era of negotiations is over.” Last year, the Brazilian presidency consolidated hundreds of existing climate initiatives – including many launched at previous COPs – into a streamlined set that could be supported and tracked under the action agenda. This included setting out more than 120 “ plans to accelerate solutions ”, to advance everything from phasing out coal to ending food waste. Tracking by UN Climate Change found that 104 of these plans had seen progress over the past year. By the end of COP31, the total number of plans had increased to 136, with new ones filling “ important gaps ”, such as early warning systems . Crucially, the plans were structured to align with the global stocktake outcomes from COP28 – such as curbing fossil fuels and tripling renewables – which all nations agreed on.  In this way, the revised action agenda is intended to explicitly support negotiated outcomes. Turkey announced 10 “ priority themes ” for the COP31 action agenda, fitting them into the existing framework. By far the most high profile was the “electrification” focus. (See: Electrification .) A book distributed at the summit by the Turkish presidency stated that a “large number of events, declarations and partnerships does not by itself constitute implementation success”. Nevertheless, the presidency did launch many new initiatives, including six voluntary 2035 targets that countries and non-state actors could sign up for.  These included “compacts” to curb the “ energy intensity ” of buildings by 25% and increase the use of “circular materials” in manufacturing to at least 15% by 2035. These initiatives attracted dozens of backers, but gained far less support than the electrification goal. Other notable initiatives pushed by the Turkish presidency include a domestic pledge for “ zero waste districts ” and an “ Antalya artificial intelligence (AI) pledge ”, which focused on curbing data-centre emissions while advancing “AI solutions for climate action”. COP31 also saw progress on two initiatives launched by COP30’s “ global mutirão ” decision that are relevant for the growth of the action agenda. The first was the “ Belém mission to 1.5 ”, which identified key priority areas for countries to meet their climate goals.  The second was the “ global implementation accelerator ”, which was formally established at COP31. This involves presidencies and experts choosing two action-agenda plans each year that are best placed to drive “ positive tipping points ” for climate action.  Cosima Cassel , E3G climate diplomacy lead, told Carbon Brief that this focus, “based on science, not just on the presidency’s priorities…is an extra step in the evolution of the action agenda”. Global climate action high-level event. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . During a COP31 session on the “accelerator”, COP30 strategy director Túlio Andrade said the Brazilian team wanted it to advance the transition “from a negotiation-focused regime to one very much focused on implementation”. The Turkish presidency also announced a new project called the “ climate implementation bridge ”, while pledging an initial $3m to support its operations. In partnership with the UN Development Programme, the bridge’s goal is to turn nations’ climate plans into “ bankable projects ” and connect them with finance.  Together, the “mission”, “accelerator” and “bridge” form part of a wider “ ecosystem ” that supporters hope will identify and support priority areas of climate action. However, the growing profile of the action agenda has resulted in pushback, with India and the Arab group arguing against any mention of it in formal negotiations. In contrast, Brazil accused the presidency of failing to significantly acknowledge these “concrete instruments and initiatives” in the proposed “Antalya pact”.  Some parties and observers are concerned that the action agenda is a diversion from parties’ obligations under UN climate treaties, such as providing climate finance. Arguing that the focus should instead be on reforming the COP process, Vanuatu climate minister Ralph Regenvanu told Carbon Brief: “Unfortunately, the action agenda has not necessarily led to action. It is indicative, again, that the COP process is broken. While people innovating and coming together to take action is good, it cannot take the place of negotiations.” Developing countries, which often have far fewer delegates , also struggle to follow all the additional activities. In a closing session , Stiell invited parties to nominate focal points so that the UN could help to “connect them with action agenda opportunities all year round”. Guilanpour noted that while “everybody says they want to focus on implementation”, within the traditional COP process this can only apply to “a very rarefied subset of obligations”, such as submitting revised NDCs. He added: “When the rest of the world hears implementation, they want to see pollution in their city going down, their energy bills going down…and that sort of implementation is in the action agenda.” Global leaders COP31’s world leaders’ summit took place during the conference’s first week from 11-12 November. Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva – whose recent re-election was widely interpreted as a timely boost for climate action and multilateralism by delegates – gave a blistering speech in the summit’s opening ceremony. He told other world leaders: “We have started talking more about weapons and tariffs than about the survival of future generations…But the planet cannot be left at the mercy of hegemonic disputes.” He told leaders that he wanted COP30 , which took place last year in the Brazilian city of Belém, to be remembered as the “COP of truth” – but that “science and multilateralism remain under attack”, adding: “It is not by chance that the incorporation of IPCC contributions into the COP negotiation process is in question. Nor is it a coincidence that climate agreements are the favourite targets of reactionary forces at COPs.” He also touted Brazil’s newly released global roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation , urging COP31 co-hosts Turkey and Australia to “ensure that the recommendations contained in these documents are disseminated and incorporated into the next global stocktake ”. In one of his final addresses in the role, UN secretary general António Guterres said that the “brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us”, adding: “Leaders – and, in particular, those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil-fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C.” Turkish leader Recep Tayyip Erdoğan used his address to call on developed countries to “take greater responsibility for emission reductions and financing” and to call out “ecocide” in Gaza. (Erdoğan faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields in Turkey on the eve of the summit.) Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley cited Carbon Brief analysis to reprimand developed countries in her address to the world leaders’ summit, telling the room: ”My friends, let us be clear: pledges are not payments. But even the promised pledges are now 70% below previous levels.” UK prime minister Andy Burnham, the only G7 leader to attend the summit, said that electrification is “how we make clean power cheap power”. He also announced the appointment of the country’s first special representative on climate security.  In total, around 70 world leaders spoke at the summit – with many major polluters missing. For the second year, the US did not send any delegates to COP. (Donald Trump took the US out of the Paris Agreement and the UN climate treaty after returning to office.) However, success for Democrats in the US midterm elections, shortly before COP31, lifted hopes that the world’s second-largest emitter could one day return to the talks. “America is all in” – a coalition of mostly Democratic governors, Congress members and local mayors – had a pavilion at COP31 and brought around 120 delegates (a figure larger than many official country delegations ). Speaking on 16 November at a pavilion event attended by Carbon Brief, Jared Huffman , a Democratic Congressional representative from California, said that the midterm results were a “clear rejection” of Trump’s “climate denial” and “wrecking ball to climate and energy policy”. He added: “The next time that we are here at a COP, it will be different…We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives. And soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change and the US will truly be officially back in as part of the negotiati[ons].” Other countries without delegations at the talks included Myanmar and Israel, according to Carbon Brief analysis. More than 92,000 registered for COP, making it potentially the largest in history, found Carbon Brief analysis. Electrification Amid a global energy crisis driven by disruption in the trade of fossil fuels, one of the biggest themes of COP31 was electrification.  Much attention was focused on which nations had signed up to a voluntary pledge to “increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035”.  For much of COP31, this was expected to be one of the main outcomes in the “Antalya pact” cover text, which ultimately failed to find agreement among parties. (See: Cover decision .) Nevertheless, some countries made public pledges of support for the target during the COP, including in a joint China-Australia statement .  COP31 president Murat Kurum told the closing plenary that “around 80” countries were behind the goal, but a full list was never published. The pledge was launched earlier in the year as a “flagship initiative of the COP31 presidency’s action agenda” – part of its wider goal to “ electrify the world ”. (See: Action agenda .) As explained on CB Connect , it drew from analysis by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), which was explicitly designed to align with the 1.5C target and support the Brazilian COP30 presidency’s “roadmap” for transitioning away from fossil fuels.  Ministers and representatives from Papua New Guinea, Antigua and Barbuda, Zambia, Germany, the Philippines and Colombia hold connected extension cables in a demonstration of their support for electrification. Credit: Carbon Brief. Towards the end of COP31, the presidency launched its “ electrification delivery package ”, capturing 14 newly announced international initiatives and other relevant projects. Among them were an industry-backed “maritime electrification goal” to increase electricity’s share of shipping’s final energy demand to 20% by 2035, as well as projects to boost grid investment, renewables in small-island states and transitions away from coal. One notable initiative was the Electrify Now Finance Coalition – launched with the backing of the COP31 and COP32 presidencies – to “mobilise over $1.2bn for clean electrification projects” in developing countries. At a coalition launch event, featuring ministers from Ethiopia, Germany, Pakistan and several other nations, Bruce Douglas , chief executive of the Global Renewables Alliance , told attendees that at least 25 nations had already put in place policies to drive electrification since the start of the “ Hormuz crisis ”. He said: “We now have the formula for success: renewable energy plus electrification equals secure, affordable and clean energy for all consumers.” China at COP31 Closing COP31 with a signal of “solidarity and multilateralism” was “more important than specific problems”, said China at the opening plenary of the summit. Its climate officials said repeatedly that not every COP required a “ new outcome ” and noted the need to “ manage expectations ”.  These comments seemed prescient when negotiations broke down at the end of COP31 over the cover decision . China had outlined its key aims for COP31 in a press conference held by Li Gao, vice-minister of ecology and environment and delegation head, in late October. These were primarily to commit developed countries to do more on mitigation and finance, as well as to address “unilateralism and protectionism” in the trade of clean-energy technologies. But Li also “commend[ed]” the presidency’s call for countries to pledge to achieve a 35% share of electricity in global final energy consumption by 2035. One of the biggest questions hovering over the COP was whether China would officially support the pledge, which was incorporated into the failed cover text .  While observers had told Carbon Brief from early in the negotiations that it would be very likely that China would support the pledge in some form, the strongest signal came from a joint statement published with Australia in the second week. In it, the two countries “welcome[d] growing international ambition and cooperation on electrification…on a voluntary basis”, mentioning the 35 by 35 goal, as well as recognising various climate, social and economic benefits from the transition. (See: Electrification .)  China-Australia joint statement on climate change and the clean energy transition, published 20 November. Source: State Council of the People’s Republic of China . The cover text had similarly sought to “recognise that electrification has significant benefits in terms of emission reductions, energy security, energy efficiency, economic development and energy access”. The joint statement, however, did not explicitly mention fossil fuels, rather it noted “countries have different transition pathways” and the “importance of secure, affordable, reliable and resilient energy systems during the transition”. Li Shuo , director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), told Carbon Brief that the “carefully curated” language helped “firm up” support for the electrification pledge – and broader language around energy – in the final draft.  China had published a joint climate statement with the EU ahead of COP30 , as well as ones with the US ahead of COPs including COP21 , COP26 and COP28 . But, unlike these agreements, the Australia-China joint statement “mostly confirms existing relatively unambitious negotiation points and does not advance ambitions” on issues including fossil fuels and decarbonising trade, argued Prof Christoph Nedopil Wang at the University of Queensland . He told Carbon Brief: “Symbolically, it would have been more meaningful to sign a more ambitious statement before COP negotiations began.” As talks broke down at the closing plenary, China endorsed the cover text’s final draft, noting that, although it has “some concerns about the content”, it chose to accept the decision to “push forward our process and show a message of unity and collective efforts”. On 23 November, China’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying:  “We express our disappointment regarding this outcome, but believe that confidence in the multilateral process should not be lost as a result.” “China was not the main blocker for the text”, said ASPI’s Li.  He added that, in his view, even if language around transitioning away from fossil fuels had been made stronger, China would have found it acceptable. China also tried to preserve the mitigation work programme (MWP) at the closing plenary. (See: Mitigation work programme .)  In negotiations, China joined other developing countries in supporting the work programme’s extension through to 2030.  Speaking on behalf of the LMDCs, China emphasised the value of the MWP, but said it needed to “focus on how to eliminate barriers of implementation”, according to Third World Network .  These included developed countries’ lack of mitigation action and financial support, as well as unilateral trade measures, it added.  China, on behalf of the LMDCs, tried to build consensus around the MWP at the closing plenary by suggesting deleting references to the first global stocktake. However, the suggestion was rejected by Russia. Meanwhile, China continued to emphasise the need for a gradual transition away from fossil fuels throughout the COP. “‘Phasing out fossil fuels’ [淘汰化石燃料] is merely a proposition of a small number of countries and has never constituted a consensus”, climate envoy Liu Zhenmin told the Paper .  He added that the energy transition required “gradually replacing fossil fuels” with clean energy over the course of “decades” and that phasing out fossil fuels should not “become a focal point of COP31 negotiations”. A few days later and thousands of miles away, the presidents of China, the US and Russia declared at the APEC Summit that the three countries “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products” in response to global energy shocks . The China delegation office at COP31 did not respond to Carbon Brief’s request for comment on this matter.  An early push to get trade on the agenda came not from China, but from the African group . In the end, the item was not included on the agenda, though it was raised by China in negotiations on the just transition work programme , adaptation fund and standing committee on finance . The China-Australia joint statement notes “measures taken to combat climate change should not constitute a means of arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination or a disguised restriction on international trade”. Prof Nedopil Wang told Carbon Brief that Australia would be more open to compromise on language with China around cleantech trade than the EU or US, as its economy has few “domestic substitutes for China’s manufactured products”. Text on trade measures were included in the cover decision drafts, though not adopted by parties. China did also focus significant attention on the just transition work programme, which was successfully passed. (See: Just transition work programme .) Speaking at a ministerial roundtable, environment vice-minister Li said that the “just transition is one of the most important agenda items of COP31” and must be operationalised.  In negotiations, China called for the mechanism to recognise the “north-south development gap” and a dedicated body to manage the programme – opposed by the EU. More broadly, the LMDCs urged that the work programme “avoid policy prescriptions” and not be linked to the global stocktake , which they argued would risk creating new obligations. Huang Runqiu, China’s minister for ecology and environment, speaking at a high-level event on the global implementation accelerator. Credit: UNFCCC . Meanwhile, at a high-level dialogue on climate finance, watched by Carbon Brief, environment minister Huang Runqiu said that developed countries’ “climate finance commitments must be honoured and the financing gap narrowed”. Huang called for the new collective quantified goal (NCQG) to be “effectively implemented”, as well as for “establishing a common definition” for climate finance and improving accounting methodologies.  He additionally highlighted the need to improve the “quality of finance”, such as providing more grants and highly concessional loans, support for adaptation and easier access to climate finance. This was echoed by BASIC , who said that “developed countries must set a pathway towards the NCQG goal of $300bn annually” and triple adaptation finance. BASIC also said the climate finance work programme (CFWP) must “operationalise Article 9.1”. The final CFWP text was passed, but only focused on procedural matters, with mentions of tripling adaptation finance and “burden-sharing” in earlier drafts removed . Requests to expand the donor base were also deleted. China maintained its emphasis on Article 9.1 in a number of workstreams, notably through the CFWP and standing committee on finance. Carbon Brief understands that China was also one of two nations driving efforts to ensure that a dialogue on Article 2.1(c) , which ensures finance flows are “consistent” with climate action, remains open and non-binding. On adaptation finance, China underscored on behalf of the LMDCs the need to triple funds, calling for a “clear roadmap and timeline to increase the share of grants, as well as a progress-review mechanism”, said Third World Network . But, in general, ASPI’s Li says, “China’s position was right in the middle of the political spectrum” on most of the issues being negotiated, maintaining a “quiet, but self-assured posture”. An early point of discussion among delegates had been whether China could have signalled greater leadership at COP, such as by announcing a bid to host COP33. News emerged at COP31 that China had, after “ months ” of consideration, decided not to do so.  Prof Hu Bin , associate professor and director of global climate governance research at Tsinghua University ’s Institute of Climate Change and Sustainable Development, told Carbon Brief that “China, politically, is still very hesitant” to claim the role of the leading country on climate. Instead it is focusing on leading in terms of the transition on-the-ground he said, adding: “I still think the reason China doesn’t want to bid for COP33 is internal pressure – the economy is slowing down, local governments are facing lots of pressure for employment and for economic growth.”  Another way in which it was suggested China could display leadership was by helping create consensus around the IPCC’s AR7 report being published in time for the second global stocktake.  At an event at the China pavilion attended by Carbon Brief, Laurence Tubiana, key architect of the Paris Agreement, said she will “count on China to be the torchbearer for the world’s science at the second global stocktake”. But, at the same event, Prof Wang Yi argued that IPCC reports from AR1 to AR6 were “unequivocal that global warming is caused by human activity”. Wang is a professor at the Chinese Academy of Science and a lead advisor to the China delegation. This means the science is clear, “no matter” when AR7 is published, he added. China instead continued to position itself as a champion of the global south, both in negotiations and around the COP. In negotiations, it consistently aligned itself with developing country parties and groups, calling for solutions that would not “widen” the north-south gap. South-south cooperation was the subject of a high-level forum at which China’s vice-president Han Zheng spoke.  Han emphasised that “China will vigorously deepen south-south cooperation” and formally announced a new global south climate leadership training programme, according to a recording of the speech obtained by Carbon Brief. China also signed an agreement with Turkey to invest $15bn in developing 7GW of solar and wind power and 4GW of transmission capacity. This deal “could be seen as part of China’s own contribution to climate finance and accelerating the global energy transition”, even if it’s not “formally accounted”, said Kate Logan , director of the China Climate Hub and climate diplomacy at ASPI .  She added that, at a broader level, it shows that “China will continue exercising its influence through real-economy actions, even while its negotiators press for developed country accountability on finance”. Ocean Ocean advocates had several outcomes to celebrate at COP31 – and also some disappointment. Before the summit started, observers – and many parties – were hopeful of securing a strong outcome for the ocean, especially in light of the pre-COP meeting held in Pacific island states. A letter sent to the COP31 presidencies on 8 October – signed by the African group, the EU (along with its member states) and 24 other countries – called for the COP to “move sustainable ocean-based climate action from recognition to implementation”.  It said that such a move should be “backed by a clear political signal, a coherent plan for integration into the Paris Agreement ambition cycle and its existing means of implementation”. Analysis published by the World Resources Institute (WRI) on 15 November found that 95% of coastal and island countries included “at least one ocean-based action” in their national climate plans. However, it added that “more than 60% of ocean-commitment implementation depends on receiving some form of external support.” Two days later, on the “ocean, seas, nature and land use” thematic day, ministers from France and Brazil announced the launch of the “Blue NDC Challenge implementation task force” at a side event. They also welcomed 10 new countries as members of the Blue NDC Challenge – a group launched at the UN Ocean Conference in Nice, France, in June 2025 to “advance ocean-based climate action”. The same day, the COP31 presidency published the “Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact”, a high-level declaration that it said drew on feedback from parties and discussions at several events, including the UN General Assembly and the Pacific pre-COP.  The document highlights the impacts of climate change on the ocean, recognises the ocean’s importance in climate action and invites parties to strengthen their ocean work. The Antalya Ocean and Seas Compact. Source: COP31 presidency . Dr Tom Pickerell , global ocean programme director at WRI, told Carbon Brief: “It was more of a platform for collective ambition and political alignment, rather than any targets or finance coming through. We wouldn’t say no to it, but if we’d left just with that, it would have been a little bit sad.” Also on the ocean thematic day, the UK government announced a new £20m ($26.2m) funding commitment to marine protection. This comprised £11.8m ($15.5m) to the Global Fund for Coral Reefs and £9m ($11.8m) to the Global Ocean Accounts Partnership , which helps countries measure their progress towards sustainable ocean development. Towards the end of the summit, the “high-level climate-resilient coral reef commitment ” gained six new signatories: Colombia, Haiti, Jamaica, Niue, Samoa and Tuvalu. These governments “commit to protect[ing] reefs identified as having greater potential to persist through climate change”, according to a press release announcing the new countries. In the formal negotiation rooms, ocean groups were closely following discussions around the cover decision, hoping to see the ocean featured prominently there. (See: Cover decision .) Draft versions of the cover text “invite[d]” the development of a multi-year plan for future ocean and climate change dialogues, to be called the “Antalya ocean current”. It also asked for the results of these dialogues to be summarised, along with the “best available science” on the ocean, in a synthesis report that would act as an input to the second global stocktake. However, the cover decision was rejected during the closing plenary. Multiple parties used their interventions during the plenary to express their regret that the work that had been done on the ocean and climate change in the cover text would not move forward. Pickerell told Carbon Brief that while “it wasn’t a ‘blue COP’ after all”, there were still positive takeaways for the ocean. He said: “We’ve left with maybe nothing in writing, but I think we have left with genuine momentum. There does seem to be this shared ambition, to move beyond just the recognition of the ocean…There’s lots of opportunities to take this forward.” Deforestation COP31 was relatively quiet on forests, compared to last year’s summit in Belém.  The presidency held a forest leaders’ summit on 11 November, which was attended by the presidents of Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo, along with the prime ministers of the Netherlands and Norway. Much of the summit dwelled on the Brazil-led Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). Delegates speculated that the summit would yield major new pledges for the fund.  However, only $88m from philanthropies emerged as new contributions at the event. Several countries reiterated past and recent pledges.  Aruna Chandrasekhar 12 November 2026, 14:19 GMT Forest funding pledges fall short Plenary Akdeniz was ringing with applause and chants of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Lula, Lula!” as Brazil’s president approached the stage for the forest leaders’ summit yesterday evening. Lula – who told the crowd he had lost his voice –… Read more on CB Connect → At the summit, Jonas Gahr Støre, Norway’s prime minister, said:  “I am hopeful we can reach our collective goal of mobilising the initial $10bn dollars and to increase from there through next year and, with this, Norway is ready to contribute up to 20% of that total.” Norway’s “up to $3bn” loan to the fund is conditional upon it hitting the $10bn mark by the end of 2026. At the same time, Støre acknowledged that “it will take some time before payments reach the tropical forest countries and the key people who we want to support”. Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila on 15 November, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pledged “an initial contribution of up to” $393m over four years to the TFFF. This means the fund has – so far – mobilised $8.2bn from different international partners, mostly as conditional loans. This leaves it $1.8bn short of a $10bn target for public and philanthropic capital for this year.  Political economist Max Alexander Matthey told Carbon Brief that less capital to invest and fewer risks taken will “lead to a fund that will not be able to deliver on the initially promised $4 per hectare” of protected forest in participating countries, even in a best-case scenario.  Although significant attention was paid to the fossil-fuel roadmap at COP31, far less focus was given to the deforestation one. Chris Dragisic , managing director for global policy at the National Audubon Society , told Carbon Brief that, nonetheless, there were “a couple of countries” that committed to producing national forest roadmaps. She added: “Many others have said, ‘we have a national strategy already’, and they’re looking at this really as an option to accelerate progress…What, for me, is the more interesting thing is that the roadmap recatalysed political will across the board for forests, where these had fallen a little bit off the political radar.” Other forest-related commitments made at COP31 included Bolivia and Indonesia joining the Forest & Climate Leaders’ Partnership and Brazil’s announcement that it is working on an Indigenous peoples’ roadmap. The COP31 presidency also launched the voluntary “Antalya action plan” on global wildfires, which it said would help a “community of countries” to “cooperate on prevention, early warning, landscape resilience and access to resources”. On the penultimate scheduled day of the summit, more than 100 organisations – including Indigenous groups, civil society and research institutions – signed an open letter calling on countries to take the work of the deforestation roadmap forward. It also called for an “international convening” on deforestation to occur in 2027. While an initial draft of the cover text “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation , this was subsequently cut.   The final cover text – which was rejected during the closing plenary – did retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai. The text had also included a recognition of nature-based solutions as “essential climate solutions”, although there is significant controversy over their use. Language on deforestation included in the final, rejected draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC . Methane Cutting emissions of methane , the potent but short-lived greenhouse gas, appeared to have a renewed push at COP31.  This is partly due to the recent confirmation of an “ inevitable ” overshoot of the 1.5C global temperature target . (See: Cover text .)    Inger Andersen , chief of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), referred to this at a COP31 methane event :  “[Methane] leaves the atmosphere quickly, so cutting its emissions is our emergency brake to slow warming.” It is “one of the fastest, cheapest and most effective ways to check global heating in the near-term ”, said UN climate chief Simon Stiell at a 12 November event on non-CO2 greenhouse gases.  At this event, UNEP announced that its methane alert system has flagged five methane leaks across Canada, Iraq, Kazakhstan and Mexico since June 2026, allowing those countries to mitigate 125,000 tonnes of methane.  New private funding of $480m (£366m) was also pledged for action on methane and other “ super pollutants ”. Nine of the 159 countries who backed a 2021 Global Methane Pledge reaffirmed their aim to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% by 2030 at the event, which was co-hosted by Brazil, China and the UK. Belgium, Canada, France, Germany, Indonesia, Micronesia, Norway, the Netherlands and the UK endorsed this “ ministerial declaration ”, committing to accelerate action towards the 2030 goal.  Separately, Australia endorsed a COP30 statement on reducing methane emissions from fossil-fuel production.  At the beginning of the second week of COP31, Mia Mottley , the prime minister of Barbados, launched a petition calling to “reduc[e] methane emissions to near zero”.  On 11 November, the daily COP31 theme centred on “zero waste”. Emine Erdoğan , the Turkish first lady and chair of a UN advisory board on waste, launched a “ global zero waste alliance ”. This aims to “build a strong foundation for cooperation where countries learn from one another” on cutting waste, said Erdoğan at the launch event. Despite this focus, the Guardian reported before COP31 that Turkey has some of the “world’s worst landfill methane leaks”.  .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } New climate science On day one of COP31, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) presented its State of the Climate 2026 update – the latest in its annual series of reports unpacking key climate indicators. The report finds that 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record. The global average surface temperature for January-September 2026 was about 1.47C above the pre-industrial average, says the report.  It adds that El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027, further boosting global temperatures . At a press conference to launch the report on 9 November, WMO secretary general Prof Celeste Saulo warned that “this 2026-27 El Niño is off the charts ”, adding that “it is different from any El Niño that we have monitored”.  Saulo warned that “we are supercharging our weather” and that “the human and economic cost is unacceptably high”. She continued: “In 2026, millions of people were exposed to unbearable heat, leading to tens of thousands of excess deaths in Europe alone. India and Pakistan and large parts of Asia and North America suffered dangerous heatwaves. And, as we head into the southern hemisphere summer, we will see more. “The catastrophe in China and Nepal showed the dangers of high-mountain disasters for downstream communities.” She concluded with a call to improve early warning systems, stating that “sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever”. The following day, the Global Carbon Project released its latest annual assessment on CO2 emissions and carbon sinks. The 21st edition of the report, written by more than 100 experts from around the world, finds that the world is projected to emit 32.8bn tonnes of CO2 this year, marking a 0.4% decrease compared to 2025. According to the report, CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement are set to fall by around 0.4% in 2026, largely due to a 1.9% drop in emissions from oil and the energy shock triggered by the Iran conflict and the closure of the strait of Hormuz. (This follows separate analysis by Carbon Brief earlier this year suggesting there would be a 0.5% fall due to the Hormuz crisis.) Meanwhile, it finds that emissions from coal are continuing to increase slightly. (For more on the findings, read Carbon Brief’s detailed write-up of the report.) A subset of the report’s authors also published a study in Nature Climate Change on 10 November, stating that “acceleration in clean technology deployment is needed to guarantee emissions peak and subsequent decline”.  Another Nature Climate Change paper , published on the opening day of COP31, finds that regions worldwide may have already experienced around 90-94% of the warming expected when the global average reaches 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.  Food and water A number of initiatives relating to food and water were launched during COP31. “Food security” – including transforming agriculture and focusing on water and drought – was one of the priority themes in the COP31 presidency’s “ action agenda ”. (See: Action agenda .) Despite this, only a few prominent announcements arrived compared to previous years.  On 9 November, when the daily COP theme centred on food, agriculture and health, thinktank Clim-Eat launched a report on the reform of agricultural subsidies. This noted that governments spend approximately $840bn (£638bn) on support and subsidies for agriculture, a sector which majorly contributes to climate change and environmental degradation .  The report outlined ways to move these subsidies towards payments supporting soil health, public infrastructure and increasing farm incomes in a more targeted way.  On 10 November, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) launched a platform aimed at helping countries boost alignment in managing food security, water and climate action, called the “ turquoise nexus initiative “.  Led by Turkey, it will exist within the FAO’s “ food and agriculture for sustainable transformation ” (FAST) partnership, which was launched at COP27 in 2022.  This is designed to boost climate finance for the transformation of food systems, while also supporting efforts on adaptation and other issues.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkey’s agriculture minister, said the “turquoise” platform would be used to strengthen existing initiatives, rather than create new ones.  İbrahim Yumaklı, Turkish minister of agriculture, at the launch of the turquoise nexus initiative in Antalya, Turkey on 10 November. Credit: Earth Negotiations Bulletin On 11 November, Ethiopia joined a group of eight other nations in the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation (ACF), a coalition launched at COP28 in 2023.  This sent a “powerful signal that food systems belong at the heart of climate action”, given that Ethiopia is due to host COP32 next year, said Emma Williams , the head of the ACF secretariat, in a statement . NDCs On 27 October, the UNFCCC released its annual report on nationally determined contributions (NDCs). These documents outline countries’ ambitions, as agreed under the Paris Agreement, to limit greenhouse gas emissions up to 2035. Based on analysis of the latest NDCs, the report says emissions are due to decrease by around 9% by 2035, compared to 2019 levels, if all pledges are implemented – a drop from the 12% reduction estimated in last year’s report . This leaves countries “substantially off track” to limit global temperatures to 1.5C, the report says. A small number of countries announced new NDCs around the time of COP31. Argentina, Botswana, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Egypt, Guatemala, North Macedonia, Palestine and Tajikistan all submitted new pledges in November. Libya also submitted its first-ever NDC, committing to reducing its carbon emissions per unit of its gross domestic product (GDP) by 28% by 2035. Protests and access  Nearly 10,000 people marched through the streets of Antalya on Saturday 14 November, protesting climate change, genocide in Gaza and human-rights abuses in Turkey. “2.8? Unacceptable”Thousands of climate protesters are out on the streets of Antalya right now 🌎 — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-14T12:04:26.419Z The middle Saturday of COP is the summit’s traditional “protest day”.  Le Monde reported that Antalya’s protest “stood out for its scale in a country where the space for protest, both environmental and political, is narrow”. Elsewhere at the summit, Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg made her first appearance at a UN climate summit since COP26 in Glasgow in 2021. Speaking to a huddle of journalists on 12 November, she said: “The climate crisis is already here and now – and it is already a matter of life and death.  “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.” Here’s a video of Greta Thunberg speaking alongside global south activists at COP this morning. More from the speakers, including Mohammad Usrof, Sagar Dhakal, Rikki Dank and Celine Isimbi, on CB Connect: connect.carbonbrief.org/t/greta-thun… — Daisy Dunne (@daisydunne.carbonbrief.org) 2026-11-12T09:58:00.064Z She was joined by global-south campaigners, including Mohammed Usrof , a climate activist and researcher from Gaza, who called out countries that continue to supply fossil fuels to Israel, telling journalists: “Corporations continue to fuel not just genocide in Palestine, but the devastation of the world. [There is a] never-ending proliferation of fossil fuels that we are seeing the consequences all over the global majority world. “So, it’s extremely crucial here to recognise what is happening in this COP, the stakes that we are here for [and] the stakes that our lived realities essentially symbolise to these negotiations.” Other speakers alongside Thunberg included Sagar Dhakal , a young Nepalese politician, who said “there are not any words in the dictionary” to describe the catastrophic flash floods in his country earlier this year, in addition to First Nations activist Rikki Dank and Rwanda-DRC activist Celine Isimbi . COP31 was plagued with logistical problems – particularly during the summit’s opening days – forcing delegates to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to access the venue. The delays sparked serious access concerns, with the ECO newsletter – a daily bulletin put together by campaigners – writing on 11 November: “Participation is not a courtesy the presidency gives out when it’s convenient. It is written into the system. Under Article 4.1(i) of the convention, parties committed to encourage ‘the widest participation’ in this process, including by non-governmental organisations. Article 12 of the Paris Agreement calls for public participation and public access to information. Nobody added a footnote saying ‘subject to traffic conditions’.” During the first part of the final plenary on 20 November, a protester – who was wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” – was ejected after standing on a chair with a red noose around their neck. Road to COP32 and beyond At COP30 , it was agreed that COP32 in 2027 will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Under the UN’s regional rotational system for hosting COP, the country will be representing the African region . It will be the first-ever COP hosted by one of the least-developed countries . Ethiopia’s prime minister Abiy Ahmed addressed the world leaders’ summit at COP31, touting his country’s fossil fuel-free electricity grid and pledging to make finance for developing countries a central part of COP32. He told other leaders:  “Dependable finance requires cooperation, even as competition between countries grows. Yet, we discuss climate in one room, development in another, trade and finance in two more. Many of us see it in all four. In each of those rooms we should ask how we will finance the future that we have agreed to build.” (There have been some concerns that conflict in the country might affect its ability to host.) During the first week of COP31, China ruled out hosting COP33 in 2028, which is due to be held in Asia. (In August, Bloomberg reported that the world’s largest emitter was considering hosting the conference.) India had withdrawn a bid to host COP33 in April. Countries that are considering making a bid to host COP33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, according to the Guardian . In the table below, Carbon Brief has compiled key meetings and milestones leading up to COP32 in Ethiopia. 11-22 January Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction COP1 , New York May Second transitioning away from fossil fuels pre-conference , Dublin, Ireland 7-17 June Bonn climate talks , Germany 19-27 June London climate action week July Second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference , Tuvalu 8-22 September UN general assembly , New York 19-26 September New York climate week 8-19 November COP32 , Addis Ababa, Ethiopia Edited by Dr Simon Evans, Leo Hickman and Molly Lempriere. title: Truths, Lies, and Prospects for the New Cross-Strait Security Complex in the Taiwan and Luzon Straits
zh_title: 台湾吕宋海峡新的两岸安全复合体的真相、谎言与前景
summary: 下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，作者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词来表示菲律宾的巩固地位。
content:
下载整期 PDF 简介 当前霍尔木兹海峡的危机表明了战略性地缘政治瓶颈如何影响全球供应链。吕宋岛和台湾海峡也不例外。曾经被学者和政治家想象为孤立和分裂的这些西太平洋阻塞点，一旦太平洋地区爆发重大冲突，就有可能损害世界经济动脉。在去年的另一篇《全球台湾简报》文章中，笔者创造了“新的海峡两岸安全复合体”（NCSSC）一词，以表示菲律宾巩固其群岛和海上防御：将西菲律宾海（WPS）和吕宋海峡作为共同关注点，并将吕宋海峡的未来安全与台湾海峡的安全联系起来。简而言之，NCSSC指的是两岸政治体之间发生和交叉的物质、制度和认知模式。笔者认为，国家社会保障委员会并不是一个空词。它代表了多个参与者遵守的有机行动框架：包括中华人民共和国（PRC）、台湾、菲律宾、美国和日本。该框架的一个值得注意的方面是认知方面如何影响互动的物质和制度模式。
简而言之，虽然一些行为者最近正在恢复过去的真相，即菲律宾伊瓦坦人民和台湾道族人民之间的过去联系，以塑造未来的关系，但还有一些行为者也在利用过去散布谎言。这包括中华人民共和国淡化这种联系，以及对巴丹群岛的主权声索。最终，国家安全安全委员会敦促各国和其他行为者为更广泛的印太地区的未来安全议程制定更明确的政策和灵活的机制。交互框架？众所周知，菲律宾在推行其外交和安全政策方面总是得过且过。文献争论它是否有一个深思熟虑的大战略，但有一件事是肯定的：台湾的未来现在在马尼拉的视野中，因为它看到中华人民共和国不受限制的地区野心。正如菲律宾领导人的言论和官方文件所指出的那样，“被拖入潜在的冲突”是一回事。然而，认识到其在更广泛的印度太平洋地区的地缘政治重要性是另一回事。 NCSSC 是一个合理的框架，可以了解区域参与者在不久的将来和遥远的将来如何互动。最近发生的事件显示了这种互动的规律性。从积极的角度来看，我们可以看到台湾人和菲律宾人在历史和文化上如何通过海洋联系在一起。 2026年6月，来自台湾最南端岛屿兰屿的20名涛人驶入菲律宾最北端岛屿巴丹群岛玛哈涛的一个港口。
这是一段约 111 英里的旅程，乘坐的是名为 Tatala（陶族人所称）或 Tataya（巴丹群岛伊瓦坦人所称）的传统木船。陶人与伊瓦坦人之间如此深厚的联系——尽管由于殖民主义而休眠了 300 年——展示了该地区的当代人民如何通过复制这种 4000 年的移民和航海实践来讲述这些闻所未闻的故事。事实上，这种重燃提醒人们它们与南岛语系的联系。尽管缺乏高级政府官员对陶伊-伊瓦坦交流的明确支持声明，菲律宾运输安全办公室战略性地

【原文 English Original】
DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Introduction The current crisis in the Strait of Hormuz demonstrates how strategic geopolitical chokepoints can affect the global supply chain. The Luzon and Taiwan Straits are no different. Once imagined by academics and politicians to be isolated and separated, these Western Pacific chokepoints have the potential to harm the world’s economic arteries should a major conflict erupt in the Pacific Region. In a separate Global Taiwan Brief article from last year, this author coined the term, “New Cross-Strait Security Complex” (NCSSC) to denote the Philippines’ consolidation of its archipelagic and maritime defense: interlocking the West Philippine Sea (WPS) and Luzon Strait as a common concern, and linking the Luzon Strait’s future security with that of the Taiwan Strait. Put simply, NCSSC refers to the material, institutional, and cognitive patterns occurring and intersecting between the polities of the two straits. This author argues that the NCSSC is not an empty term. It represents an organic framework of action observed by multiple actors: including the People’s Republic of China (PRC), Taiwan, the Philippines, the United States, and Japan. One notable dimension of this framework comes with how the cognitive aspect affects the material and institutional patterns of interactions. Simply put, while some actors are recently recovering truths of the past—namely, the past connection between the Philippines’ Ivatan people, and Taiwan’s Tao people—to shape the future relations, still others are also using the past to spread lies. This includes the PRC’s downplay of that connection, and claims over the Batanes Islands. Ultimately, the NCSSC impels states and other actors to produce clearer policies with flexible mechanisms for the future security agenda in the broader Indo-Pacific region. A Framework of Interaction? The Philippines is known to muddle through in pursuing its foreign and security policies. The literature debates whether or not it has a deliberate grand strategy , yet one thing is certain: the future of Taiwan is now in Manila’s sights as it sees the PRC’s regional ambitions unrestrained. “To be dragged into a potential conflict”—as noted by Philippine leaders’ rhetoric and official documents —is one thing. However, to appreciate its geopolitical importance in the broader Indo-Pacific is another. The NCSSC serves as a sensible framework to see how regional actors might interact in the immediate and distant future. Recent events show the regularity of such interaction. On a positive note, we can see how Taiwanese and Filipinos are historically and culturally linked by the seas. In June 2026, 20 Tao people from Orchid Island (Lanyu, 蘭嶼 ), Taiwan’s southernmost island, sailed into a port in Mahatao, Batanes, the Philippines’ northernmost island. This was a journey of about 111 miles using a traditional wooden boat known as Tatala (as known by the Tao people) or Tataya (as known by the Ivatans of Batanes). Such deep connections between the Taos and Ivatans—although dormant for 300 years due to colonialism—demonstrates how contemporary peoples of this region are making these unheard stories heard by replicating this 4000-year practice of migration and seafaring. Indeed, such rekindling serves as a reminder of their Austronesian linkage. Though lacking an explicit supportive statement of the Tao-Ivatan exchange by higher government officials, the Philippines’ Office for Transportation Security strategically framed its press release about Manila’s resolve to “ensure that the country’s northern maritime gateways remain protected and efficient” in the case of “welcoming communities.” Image: The Batanes Strait, between Taiwan and the northern Philippines. In 2026, PRC government institutions began to advance the claim that the Batanes Islands (part of the Philippines) were Chinese territory, based on the extension of the continental shelf from Taiwan. (Image source: Google Maps ) Interestingly, two Chinese officials— Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan, and Consul and Head of Post Li Xiaoyan of the Chinese Consulate in Laoag, Ilocos Norte— arrived in Batanes on the same day as the Tao people’s arrival for an “official visit” to the province’s officials. On the one hand, this visit serves to remind Philippine officials of Manila’s “One-China Policy.” On the other hand, it also means that Beijing is now playing into the logic of the NCSSC, which serves as a prognosis for broader regional tensions. Some academics from the PRC contest the “ Out of Taiwan” theory of Austronesian linkage between the Tao and Ivatan peoples. Rather, they prefer to propagate Beijing’s narrative of historic rights over Taiwan, contending that these indigenous peoples came instead from mainland southern China. In July 2026, a Global Times article reported that several PRC-based academics at an academic symposium in Jinan University ( 暨南大學 ) asserted that the Batanes Islands “are legally China’s sovereign territory and form a natural geographic extension of China’s Taiwan island,” on the basis of the 1898 Treaty of Paris and the so-called “Japan-Philippines maritime delimitation talks.” In other words, by virtue of PRC’s historic claims on Taiwan and the Tao’s linkage to the Ivatans, Batanes is allegedly an integral part of the PRC. Philippine government officials have rebuked such PRC academic’s claims on Batanes. For instance, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. noted at the sidelines of the West Philippine Sea summit that such talking points by PRC academics validated his agency’s assessment that Beijing wants to control the Western Pacific. Moreover, given that there is no serious legal basis for such claims, Teodoro noted that “it’s a joke.” Separately, Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro noted that the government would not listen to unofficial channels, while her agency’s spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said that “flights of fancy should not be dignified with a response” since “the Philippines’ sovereignty over Batanes is settled and not up for debate.” Batanes’ lone District House Representative, Ciriaco Gato Jr., similarly rebuked such claims, noting that “any challenge to our status is not merely a geopolitical provocation; it is an affront to our identity that we will not tolerate.” The Philippine’s National Historical Commission (NHC) debunked the Chinese scholarly claims, noting that there is a continuous shelf extending from Northern Luzon through the Babuyan and Batanes Islands and into parts of the Taiwan archipelago based on “current satellite and oceanographic data.” There were also reported circulations among Chinese social media apps last year suggesting that the Philippine province of Palawan—which puts the Municipality of Kalayaan in the WPS under its jurisdiction—is allegedly part of China, by virtue of Ming-era Admiral Zheng He’s explorations. At the macro-level, the Philippine government recognizes that such Chinese talking points are reinforced by foreign influence and malign interference (FIMI) operations —various kinetic activities that aim to alter Filipino solidarity in favor of PRC’s narratives. All Set for the Future? These latest events demonstrate that the framework of interaction demonstrated by the NCSSC does not only involve material and institutional aspects, but also the most basic of human cognitive elements—identity, historical memory, and people-to-people linkage—which are all essential to make the case for brokering the regional commons. They also point to a common denominator: the PRC’s irredentist and unrestrained expansion. However, the NCSSC also opens novel methods for various stakeholders to explore opportunities to assert their agency. The first opportunity refers to cognitive patterns. Whether by constraints or deliberate choice, the Taiwanese government has yet to make any comments on the claim by PRC-based academics regarding Batanes. While ignoring Chinese talking points against the Philippines may sound risk-averse, there is an equal harm inherent in isolating these comments outside the PRC’s broader FIMI operations. Taiwan’s political and security apparatuses would be well advised to invest their attention in curating counter-responses. Moreover, both Manila and Taipei must also leverage linkages between Filipino and Taiwanese cultural communities, academics, think tanks, and civil society organizations, to counter the PRC’s FIMI operational logic. The second opportunity refers to institutional patterns. Since Taiwan is de facto limited in its diplomatic options, the Philippines—with its rapidly expanding strategic partnerships—could serve as a node of a broader security network by framing the Luzon and Taiwan Straits as strategic nerves that cannot be unilaterally occupied by one regional hegemon. Rather, the Straits represent a politically plural area in which to enforce a rules-based international order. This would mean enhancing logistical points of entry and exchange through increased port security, diversifying areas of cooperation between their respective coast guards, fisheries agreements, and anti-piracy and anti-smuggling frameworks, among others. Moreover, while Filipino and American officials argue that Balikatan exercises are solely for Philippine defense, and not intended as a stage for a Taiwan contingency, Filipino and other regional scholars and analysts otherwise note that they are not mutually exclusive. Here, wargaming centers by academics and think tanks can intensify stress-testing assumptions into wider grand strategic considerations, which ripple into Track 1.5/2 dialogues and influence public opinion. The third opportunity refers to material patterns. So far, it is microchip discourse which catches the main attention of the PRC, the US, and other global players on this NCSSC. Minilateral forums serve as cost-efficient avenues in addressing shortcomings of multilateral forums that have been hijacked by PRC’s “Global South Champion” narrative. Moreover, informal talks—like the “Smart Harbor” forum in December 2025 between Taipei and Philippine officials—demonstrate the balance between strategic autonomy and risk-aversion. The Luzon Economic Corridor, which feeds into the US’s Pax Silica initiative to counter the PRC’s World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), are both welcome developments. Taiwan has stated on separate occasions that it is willing to expand economic corridors with the Philippines, either through its proposed “ Silicon Prosperity Initiative ” or as an external node with Pax Silica . So far, Pax Silica has not been well received by most Filipinos, largely due to the lack of an accurate and transparent blueprint, which in turn caused fear among local communities. So far, the Philippines rejection of a diplomatic immunity bargain by the United States in the proposed Pax Silica compound in North Luzon are very well noted points to rebuke PRC narratives of the Philippines “as an American Puppet.” However, the broader goal must be the ability of the Philippines to become a formidable node of the global supply chain through state-led development—not “independent” for its own sake—while addressing local woes. In sum, there is a need for more assertive Philippine counterproposals to serve the country’s industrial interests if it is to become Taiwan’s capable partner. Strategic uncertainty will continue to pervade the 21 st century, and the new geopolitical reality of the NCSSC has now emerged around which all stakeholders must carefully design their approach. They must set clear policy interests while maintaining flexible mechanisms. As for the Philippines and Taiwan, they have an opportunity to set their shared path by modeling such interactions. The main point: The Philippines is becoming more relevant to the future of Taiwan’s security, as the two island states find their security concerns ever-more connected. It is time for all stakeholders to integrate the New Cross-Strait Security Complex as part of the broader regional security architecture. They should and can achieve this through clearer policies, with flexible and responsive mechanisms for future interaction. title: Double Dragon: How Taiwan and South Korea Can Collaborate through Chips
zh_title: 双龙：台湾和韩国如何通过芯片进行合作
summary: 下载整期 PDF 台湾和韩国是亚洲四小龙中人口和经济总量最大的两个国家，两国是激烈的竞争对手，尤其是在半导体制造业。但它们对中国市场的共同依赖已成为双方都无法单独解决的弱点。每个人都控制着全球半导体制造的关键节点，它们共同可能构成全球硬件生态系统的瓶颈。台北和首尔应该合作开拓新市场并与大国进行谈判。他们在一起拥有任何人都无法运用的影响力
content:
下载整期 PDF 台湾和韩国是亚洲四小龙中人口和经济总量最大的两个国家，两国是激烈的竞争对手，尤其是在半导体制造业。但它们对中国市场的共同依赖已成为双方都无法单独解决的弱点。每个人都控制着全球半导体制造的关键节点，它们共同可能构成全球硬件生态系统的瓶颈。台北和首尔应该合作开拓新市场并与大国进行谈判。他们在一起所拥有的影响力是任何一个人都无法单独有效地运用的。台湾和韩国是竞争对手，也是伙伴，长期以来一直是死对头。 1992年首尔从台北转而承认北京这一相对较新的记忆，给许多台湾人留下了挥之不去的背叛感，因为韩国是亚洲最后一个与台湾断绝外交关系的国家。据称，在2000年代和2010年代，韩国三星电子推行“杀台”计划，旨在削弱台湾的芯片制造能力。此外，2010年亚运会跆拳道比赛的有争议的裁判，也被称为“索克门”，严重侵蚀了双边的公众善意。 2012年，富士康创始人郭台铭在讨论与三星的竞争时，使用具有种族主义贬义的“高丽棒子”来指代韩国人，引发强烈批评，进一步助长韩国的反台情绪。
鉴于这段痛苦的历史和所涉及的非常现实的财务利益，韩国和台湾芯片公司的竞争常常被相互对抗的感觉所掩盖。过去，外部试图协调台北和首尔的芯片政策——例如总统乔·拜登的“芯片4联盟”概念——失败了，因为他们没有充分考虑台湾和韩国领先芯片制造商之间激烈竞争的逻辑。然而，不健康的竞争和民族主义不应该让任何一方蒙蔽双眼。如今，两个邻近的东亚民主国家及其制造业冠军之间的协同关系比许多人想象的要强得多。台裔英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋近期分别于5月底和6月初连续访问台湾和韩国，受到两地热烈欢迎。这样的反应说明了两国经济在当今半导体行业中的相互联系和互补程度有多深。黄先生还因其对促进美韩关系的贡献而被授予今年的詹姆斯·范弗利特奖。在经济上，亚洲邻国建立了持久的关系。 2025年，韩国是台湾第三大贸易伙伴，台湾是韩国第四大贸易伙伴。此外，两个经济体之间已经存在部分劳动分工。
台湾公司，尤其是台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司（台积电、台湾积体电路制造股份有限公司）制造先进的逻辑芯片，而韩国的三星和 SK 海力士则在存储器领域占据主导地位。这些公司（以及两国）是当今人工智能革命不可或缺的一部分，无论是在训练人工智能模型还是为数据中心提供服务方面。到2025年，两国经济体的双边芯片贸易额将超过600亿美元，其中台湾的先进逻辑芯片支持韩国人工智能计算基础设施的快速发展，而台湾则封装了许多韩国制造的高带宽内存（HBM）芯片。 2025年台湾进口额约493亿美元

DOWNLOAD FULL ISSUE PDF Taiwan and South Korea, the two largest of the Four Asian Dragons by population and economic output, are fierce rivals, especially in the semiconductor manufacturing industry. But their common reliance on China’s market has become a vulnerability that neither can address alone. Each controls crucial nodes of global semiconductor manufacturing, and together they could constitute a chokepoint in the global hardware ecosystem. Taipei and Seoul should collaborate to open new markets and negotiate with major powers. Together, they have leverage that neither one can wield so effectively alone. Rivals, but Also Partners Taiwan and South Korea have long been bitter rivals. The relatively recent memory of Seoul switching recognition from Taipei to Beijing in 1992 has left a lingering sense of betrayal among many Taiwanese, as South Korea was the last country in Asia to end diplomatic relations with Taiwan. In the 2000s and 2010s, South Korea’s Samsung Electronics allegedly pursued a “kill Taiwan” plan aimed at undermining Taiwan’s chipmaking capabilities. Furthermore, the contested judgment in the taekwondo competition at the 2010 Asian Games, also called “ Sockgate ,” sharply eroded bilateral public goodwill. In 2012, Foxconn founder Terry Gou (郭台銘), while discussing competition with Samsung, used the derogatory racist slur, gaoli bangzi (高麗棒子), to refer to Koreans, prompting strong criticism and further fueling anti-Taiwanese sentiment in South Korea. Given this bitter history and the very real financial stakes involved, the South Korean and Taiwanese chip firm rivalry is often shaded by feelings of mutual antagonism. In the past, outside attempts to align Taipei and Seoul’s chip policies—such as President Joe Biden’s “Chip 4 Alliance” concept —fell short because they did not adequately reckon with the logic of heated competition between leading Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers. However, unhealthy rivalry and nationalism should not blind either side. The two neighboring East Asian democracies, together with their manufacturing champions, have a far more synergistic relationship today than many assume. Taiwanese American Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) recent consecutive visits to Taiwan and South Korea in late May and early June, respectively, garnered warm welcomes in both places. Such a reaction speaks to how deeply interconnected and complementary the two economies have become in today’s semiconductor industry. Huang was also awarded this year’s James A. Van Fleet Award for his contributions to the promotion of US-South Korea relations. Economically, the Asian neighbors have built enduring ties. In 2025, South Korea was Taiwan’s third-largest trading partner, while Taiwan was South Korea’s fourth-largest . Furthermore, a partial division of labor already exists between the two economies. Taiwanese firms, notably Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC, 台灣積體電路製造股份有限公司), manufacture advanced logic chips , while South Korea’s Samsung and SK Hynix dominate memory. These companies (and both countries) are integral to today’s AI revolution, both for training AI models and supplying data centers. The two economies conducted over USD 60 billion in bilateral chip trade in 2025, with Taiwan’s advanced logic chips supporting rapid AI compute infrastructure development in South Korea, while Taiwan packages many South Korean-made high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips. In 2025, Taiwan imported around USD 49.3 billion worth of integrated circuits from South Korea, representing 37.7 percent of Taiwan’s chip imports, far more than from any other country. South Korea accounted for a smaller but still significant share of Taiwan’s integrated circuit exports , around USD 18.4 billion, or 8.8 percent. Shared Challenges Yet despite this growing industrial interdependence, Taiwan and South Korea remain exposed to the same strategic vulnerability: both of them depend heavily on China as a major downstream market for their chips. China’s booming electronics industry consumes vast quantities of semiconductor chips for everything from iPhones to appliances to AI data centers. In 2025, 51.2 percent of Taiwan’s chip exports went to mainland China or Hong Kong, while 41.7 percent of South Korean chip exports headed to the PRC. Such overwhelming reliance on one market—especially one that is actively subsidizing its own domestic chip manufacturers to gradually reduce foreign dependence—carries substantial economic security risk. SK Hynix, Samsung, and TSMC may eventually lose much of China’s demand to state-backed Chinese firms. Moreover, Beijing’s increasingly aggressive security posture and willingness to coerce smaller economies make China a fundamentally unreliable customer. Taiwan and South Korea have long recognized this problem, and each has pursued its own trade reorientation over the past decade. Taipei launched the “New Southbound Policy” under former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) in 2016. Seoul followed in 2017 by initiating its “New Southern Policy” under then-president Moon Jae-in. These policies succeeded in deepening economic relations with other markets—especially those in Southeast Asia—but have failed to fundamentally reorient chip exports away from China. At the time, the political impetus and market opportunities were simply insufficient. Image: A semiconductor chip manufactured by SK Hynix, one of South Korea’s major chip manufacturers. Taiwan and South Korea manufacturers have faced intense competition qin the market for advanced chips. (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) How to Team Up Through Chips Today, Seoul and Taipei cannot afford to go it alone. Reducing the relative weight of the Chinese market for their chip exports is not only a security imperative; it is an economic necessity as China’s indigenous chip ecosystem gains ground . Building on the complementary strengths of their semiconductor industries, South Korea and Taiwan could establish an industry-led bilateral working group led by their chip giants—TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix—to coordinate semiconductor trade and investment policy. Given the absence of formal diplomatic relations, a direct government-to-government framework with ministerial leadership would not be realistic. However, the sheer economic and monetary weight of these private firms and their close ties to their respective governments would give a cooperative framework substantial influence and credibility. For instance, Taiwan’s National Development Fund is a major shareholder in TSMC, while TSMC founder and former CEO Morris Chang led Taiwan’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) delegation seven times between 2006 and 2023. Similarly, given its strong relationships with Korean chip firms, the Lee Jae Myung administration has a record of leveraging its commercial involvement to pursue decisive political objectives . For instance, ahead of the August 2026 election in South Korea for Democratic Party leadership, Lee promoted a major semiconductor cluster in Jeolla Province backed by planned investment from Samsung and SK Hynix. The initiative benefited one of Lee’s cabinet officials, Kim Min-seok, helping him win the election for party leader to replace Lee’s prominent rival within the party, Jung Chung-rae. Critics accused the administration of using corporate investment to tilt politics in Lee’s favor. Yet, this example demonstrates that Seoul maintains substantial influence over its domestic semiconductor industry—and could work effectively with those firms to facilitate de facto economic collaboration with their Taiwanese counterparts that prioritizes national rather than private interests. Similarly, TSMC — which was established with Taipei’s financial and political backing in 1987 — retains close ties to Taiwan’s political leadership. Taiwanese and South Korean industry associations and companies would provide the institutional backbone of the working group and serve as the primary channel for bilateral engagement, with which the governments could easily and regularly engage. Trade and economic government officials could participate discreetly at the working level or through the two sides’ representative offices. More senior officials would have the opportunity to speak directly in private meetings alongside multilateral institutions in which both are represented, such as the APEC, to coordinate the working group. Some level of unofficial government contact is prudent to ensure that the nominally private sector working group advances the interests of South Korea and Taiwan as a whole, as well as those of their chip firms. This working group would have two primary aims: (1) to develop a common strategy to cultivate new markets; and (2) to coordinate negotiations on new trade and investment agreements with major economies from a position of greater strength. One Strategy, One Face Taiwanese and South Korean chips flow primarily to three sectors: cloud computing infrastructure; consumer goods such as electronics , appliances and automobiles ; and telecommunications equipment. Yet China’s massive output in all three categories has created a gravitational pull that has been hard for Taiwanese and Korean chip firms to escape. As a result, any joint Taiwan-South Korea strategy for cultivating overseas markets and negotiating trade agreements must go beyond setting up chip packaging facilities or even fabs. They must push for a broader set of economic reforms in those markets that will facilitate the rapid development of consumer electronics manufacturing and cloud computing infrastructure. India holds the most potential. Unlike in Southeast Asia , Chinese investment and 5G telecommunications penetration are fairly low , and the country has massive room for growth. Individual Taiwanese and South Korean firms such as Foxconn, Samsung, and Hyundai have had success with particular projects that received special Indian government attention and support. Indeed, the Indian government has repeatedly identified electronics, automobiles, and semiconductors as key sectors to bolster India’s manufacturing output. But India’s complex regulatory environment, bureaucratic proceduralism, infrastructure development bottlenecks, and sometimes counterproductive labor laws mean that India’s operating environment remains very difficult for foreign investors. [1] As a result, India has failed to generate an electronics manufacturing ecosystem—and chip demand—that can rival China’s. By speaking with one voice to New Delhi as the only two economies capable of helping fulfill India’s ambitions in electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, Seoul and Taipei might make greater progress in pressing for reforms in India than either could alone. They might also open greater access for Taiwanese and South Korean firms to a more populated market than China—one which has yet to expend its demographic dividend. The same logic applies to Taiwan’s and South Korea’s policies vis-à-vis the United States. In recent years, successive US administrations have pressed Taiwanese and South Korean chipmakers to expand manufacturing on American soil, from the Biden Administration’s CHIPS and Science Act to the Trump Administration’s greater demands for investments in the United States. Washington’s desire to reshore enough chip production to sustain its defense capabilities and economic system in a supply shock is a rational pursuit. However, as long as key inputs, downstream packaging, and testing still occur outside of the United States, domestic chip fabrication alone is inadequate to ensure US economic resilience. Moreover, a substantial share of the world’s chips still end up in electronics made in Asia. Even if the United States can ensure a bare minimum supply at home for military use and cloud services providers, it will have to look beyond its borders for sufficient demand to make US chip production economical in the long run. Image: Then-President Joseph Biden and then-President Yoon Suk-yeol visiting a Samsung semiconductor plant in South Korea (May 2022), (Image source: Wikimedia Commons ) More recent US administrations have focused on boosting foreign investment in the United States. A Washington willing to subordinate political and geostrategic partnerships in favor of a maximum reshoring effort might seek to play Taipei and Seoul against each other by inducing them to pledge ever greater semiconductor investments. This tactic could gradually hollow out the manufacturing capacity underpinning their respective “silicon shields,” leaving both more vulnerable to security threats from China in the long run — even if the most advanced logic chips are still produced in Taiwan. Instead of competing to offer ever-larger investments and concessions, Taipei and Seoul should coordinate the scale, terms, and technological scope of their US investments. Rather than sending an ultimatum to Washington, Taipei and Seoul could provide a roadmap for a sustained Taiwan-South Korea-US trilateral partnership on semiconductor innovation and fabrication to support US-led AI stack dominance (which covers the whole production chain from critical minerals and energy to semiconductors and telecommunications equipment, upon which the development and rollout of AI software relies). This triangle would be based on mutual trust and common economic and security interests. This would be far more beneficial to all involved—including the United States—than haphazard investment pledges. Targeted investments would complement ongoing economic security projects (such as the Hanwha Philly Shipyard in Philadelphia ) and help anchor chip fab suppliers in the United States. They would also allow Taiwanese and South Korean chip firms to better serve their US customers; indeed, this was part of the rationale that made the initial TSMC plant in Arizona feasible. More direct cooperation between Taipei, Seoul, and Washington may also allow all three parties to identify and capitalize on new production synergies of which US policymakers may not be aware. The main point : Ongoing commercial rivalry and nationalist sentiments show that the Taiwan-South Korea partnership will not be easy. But in continuing to work alone—and sometimes at odds—Taipei and Seoul are leaving leverage on the table that could secure their symbiotic prosperity for years to come. [1] Devesh Kapur and Arvind Subramanian, A Sixth of Humanity: Independent India’s Development Odyssey (Gurugram: HarperCollins Publishers India, 2025). 下载整期 PDF 封面图片：台北市长电视辩论主办方提供照片（来源：记者） 编者注：这是两部分系列中的第二篇文章。第一篇文章《首都之战：2026年台北市长竞选内幕（上）》于10月30日发表。作为现任台北市长的中国国民党蒋万安面临着与民进党提名候选人沈伯洋连任的巨大压力。尽管他们的背景和公众形象相似，但他们的政治声誉、政策问题立场和竞选风格却截然不同。随着11月28日大选（台湾规模较大的“九合一”地方选举的一部分）临近，全岛都在关注“洋流”或“洋流”（见下文）是否会导致未来四年不同的政治格局。竞争候选人的背景 作为目前国内外关注焦点的台北市长竞选的两位领先候选人，蒋和沉在经历和公众形象方面有一些惊人的相似之处。蒋和沈都与台北有着深厚的渊源，因为他们都在这座城市长大，并就读于著名的建国中学，该中学被誉为台湾最好的男子高中。
他们杰出的高等教育背景也强化了他们的精英形象：蒋获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位（LL.M.）和法学博士学位（J.D.），而沉获得了宾夕法尼亚大学法学硕士学位和法学博士学位。加州大学欧文分校犯罪学、法律和社会学位。在台湾政治中，学历和教育资历起着“极其重要”的作用。台湾的竞选广告牌、传单和其他宣传材料往往侧重于突出候选人的教育资历而不是其他特征，因为许多台湾选民将候选人的教育水平和母校的声望视为其执政能力的指标。台湾知名政界人士大多至少拥有硕士学位，而拥有博士学位的人竞选立法或市长级别的公职也很常见。因此，毫不奇怪，在2026年竞选台北市长的六名候选人中，其中五人拥有博士学位。学位或法学博士（第六名候选人拥有硕士学位）。此外，蒋、沈均是各自政党的中年一代，年龄相近，政治履历也较新。
国民党和民进党的重要人物均年龄偏大，据观察，当地政客的平均年龄正在增加。相比之下，两位台北市长候选人被认为是各自政党的“新鲜血液”。 2015年当选立委，2020年赢得台北市长选举；沉在2023年首次进入立法院。无论2026年的选举结果如何，他们都将成为未来十年各自政治阵营中的后起之秀。尽管有上述共同点，两人的政治声誉和道路却截然不同。例如，蒋介石的家族关系
